issues.legal_issue: Administrative bias and bad faith must be assessed from the circumstances of the individual case, and only an objectively supported real likelihood or substantial possibility of bias makes administrative action unsustainable.
material_facts: The former chief administrative officer referred two matters involving senior officials to an independent investigative agency after the head of government directed that they be referred.

The new government withdrew those referrals after the investigative agency had registered cases and later issued a disciplinary charge-sheet against the former chief administrative officer for making the referrals.
The record did not provide cogent evidence that the former chief administrative officer acted from personal spite or ill will.
issues.conclusion: A mere apprehension, conjecture, or general allegation of bias or bad faith is insufficient; the court must find a real likelihood or substantial possibility of bias from the circumstances, assessed objectively and case by case.
issues.legal_principle: Fairness is synonymous with reasonableness, and bias is assessed by whether a reasonable person would infer a real likelihood of bias; surmise or conjecture is insufficient. A substantial possibility of bias can invalidate administrative action. Bad faith requires cogent evidence and ordinarily involves an intentional wrongful act without just cause or excuse. The Court relied on Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam v. Girija Shankar Pant, S. Parthasarthy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, Rattan Lal Sharma v. Managing Committee, Dr. Hari Ram (Co-education) Higher Secondary School, Jones Brothers (Hunstanton) Ltd. v. Stevens, Bromage v. Prosser, Reg. v. Gough, Pinochet, and Locabail (U.K.) Ltd. v. Bayfield Properties Ltd.

predicates.administrative_action_review: The proceeding asks a court to review action taken by an administrative authority.
predicates.objective_circumstances_show_substantial: The circumstances provide objective grounds for a reasonable person to infer a real likelihood or substantial possibility that the authority is biased.

issues.definition: When administrative action is reviewed and objective circumstances show a substantial possibility of bias, the action is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A disciplinary charge-sheet may be quashed before completion of the inquiry when concrete circumstances show that the inquiry is biased or predetermined, notwithstanding the usual requirement that the employee first respond to the charges.
material_facts: The charge-sheet accused the former chief administrative officer of misconduct in referring two matters to an independent investigative agency.
The new government had withdrawn the referrals after cases were registered and then initiated disciplinary proceedings against the officer.
Before the deadline for the officer to reply to the charge-sheet had expired, the head of government publicly stated that a judge would look into the charges against him.
The Court considered that announcement an indication that the inquiry would proceed irrespective of the officer’s reply and found justification for the criticism that the authorities were biased.
The High Court quashed the charge-sheet and proceedings, and the Supreme Court upheld that decision.
issues.conclusion: The charge-sheet and disciplinary proceedings were properly quashed because the circumstances supported a finding of bias and a predetermined inquiry; the appeals were dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Ordinarily, an employee should reply to a charge-sheet and raise available objections before the disciplinary authority, and a court should not intervene prematurely. However, the Court may intervene at the outset where malice or bias is established or the inquiry would be a farcical exercise. The disciplinary authority must consider the employee’s reply and decide whether a further inquiry is warranted. The Court relied on Union of India v. Ashok Kacker for the ordinary rule against premature challenges and applied the principles of fairness, bias, and real likelihood of bias discussed in Kumaon Mandal Vikas Nigam v. Girija Shankar Pant, S. Parthasarthy v. State of Andhra Pradesh, and Rattan Lal Sharma v. Managing Committee, Dr. Hari Ram (Co-education) Higher Secondary School.

predicates.disciplinary_charge_sheet_challenge: An employee asks a court to set aside a disciplinary charge-sheet before the inquiry is completed.
predicates.concrete_circumstances_show_prejudgment: The authority’s conduct, including publicly committing to proceed with an inquiry before considering the employee’s response, provides concrete grounds to find that the inquiry is biased or predetermined.

issues.definition: When an employee challenges a disciplinary charge-sheet before the inquiry is completed and concrete circumstances show prejudgment, the charge-sheet and proceedings are quashed.
